title: Type Coercion and Equality
description: How == quietly converts operand types, why === usually wins, and the handful of exceptions worth memorizing.

blocks.content: `===` compares value and type with no conversion. `==` first coerces operands toward a common type using a fixed set of rules (e.g. comparing against `null`/`undefined` only matches each other; numbers vs strings convert the string to a number) before comparing. `Object.is()` behaves like `===` except it treats `NaN` as equal to itself and distinguishes `+0` from `-0`.
keyPoints: `null == undefined` is `true`, but `null === undefined` is `false` — this is one of the few places `==` is arguably useful (checking for 'either null or undefined').
Object equality (`===` or `==`) always compares references, never structural/deep content, for both operators.
`NaN === NaN` is `false` — use `Number.isNaN()` or `Object.is(x, NaN)` to actually detect NaN.

blocks.code:
'5' + 1;      // '51'  (+ concatenates when either side is a string)
'5' - 1;      // 4     (- always coerces to numbers)
0 == false;   // true  (loose equality coerces)
0 === false;  // false (strict equality does not)
Object.is(NaN, NaN); // true
blocks.explanation: `+` is the one arithmetic operator that also means string concatenation, which is why it coerces differently from `-`, `*`, `/`.

blocks.question: What does `[] == false` evaluate to, and why?
blocks.answer: true.
blocks.explanation: `==` coercion rules convert both sides toward numbers when one side is a boolean: `false` becomes `0`, and the empty array `[]` is first converted to a primitive via `toString()` (yielding `""`), then `""` converts to `0` — so the comparison becomes `0 == 0`, which is true. This is exactly the kind of surprising chain that makes `===` the recommended default: it never engages this conversion machinery at all.

title: ES6 Classes and Private Fields
description: Class syntax as sugar over prototypes, and real, language-enforced privacy with #private fields.

blocks.content: `class` syntax builds on the same prototype-based inheritance JavaScript already had — methods declared in a class body are installed on `ClassName.prototype` and shared by every instance, exactly like the manual `Constructor.prototype.method = ...` pattern. `#privateField` syntax adds true, engine-enforced privacy: unlike a `_conventionallyPrivate` property, code outside the class cannot read, write, or even detect a `#field`'s existence.
keyPoints: Class methods are non-enumerable on the prototype, unlike properties assigned in the constructor.
`#private` fields are scoped to the class body lexically — even a subclass cannot access a parent's `#field` directly.
`static` members belong to the class itself, not instances, and are commonly used for factory methods or shared constants.

blocks.explanation: `#balance` cannot be read, mutated, or even referenced from outside `BankAccount` — this is real privacy enforced by the JavaScript engine, not just a naming convention like `_balance`.

title: ES Modules and Dynamic Import
description: Static import/export boundaries, and using dynamic import() for runtime code-splitting.

blocks.content: ES modules use static `import`/`export` declarations, resolved and validated before any module code runs — this static structure is what lets bundlers tree-shake unused exports. `import()` (as a function call, not a declaration) is dynamic: it returns a Promise that resolves to the module's namespace object, and it's the standard mechanism behind route-level and on-demand code splitting.
keyPoints: Static imports are hoisted and resolved at parse time; dynamic `import()` can appear anywhere, including inside conditionals and event handlers.
A dynamically-imported chunk is only downloaded when the `import()` call actually executes — this is exactly how Angular's `loadComponent`/`loadChildren` route lazy-loading works under the hood.
Circular ES module dependencies are allowed but can leave one side seeing a partially-initialized export if not handled carefully.

blocks.explanation: The heavy charting library's bytes never reach the browser until `openAnalytics()` is actually called, keeping the initial bundle small.

blocks.question: Why can bundlers tree-shake unused exports from static ES modules but generally cannot from CommonJS (`require`/`module.exports`)?
blocks.answer: Static `import`/`export` declarations form a graph that's fully knowable without executing any code — a bundler can see exactly which named exports are imported and drop the rest. CommonJS's `require()` and `module.exports` are just regular function calls and object mutations that happen at runtime, so a bundler generally can't prove which properties of an exported object are actually used without executing the module.
blocks.explanation: This static analyzability is one of the concrete practical reasons the ecosystem moved from CommonJS to ES modules, beyond just syntax preference.

title: Memory Management and Garbage Collection
description: How the engine decides what to reclaim, and the common patterns that accidentally keep things alive.

blocks.content: JavaScript engines garbage-collect by tracing reachability from a set of roots (global object, active call stacks, closures still in scope) — anything unreachable from a root is eventually reclaimed. "Memory leaks" in JS almost always mean something is unintentionally still reachable, not that the engine failed to collect it. `WeakMap`/`WeakSet` hold their keys weakly, so entries don't by themselves keep an object alive.
keyPoints: Common leak sources: event listeners never removed, `setInterval` timers never cleared, module-level caches that grow unbounded, and closures capturing more than they need.
GC timing is nondeterministic and not something application code controls or should rely on for cleanup ordering.
Use `WeakMap` to attach metadata to an object (e.g. a DOM node) without preventing that object from being garbage-collected once nothing else references it.

blocks.question: A single-page app's memory usage climbs steadily every time the user navigates between two routes, never coming back down. How would you find and fix the leak?
blocks.answer: Take heap snapshots (DevTools Memory tab) before and after several navigation cycles and diff retained object counts to find what's growing. Look specifically at event listeners attached to long-lived targets (`window`, `document`) that aren't removed on route/component teardown, timers (`setInterval`/`setTimeout`) never cleared, and subscriptions (RxJS, WebSocket) never unsubscribed. Fix by cleaning up in the component/route's teardown hook (e.g. Angular's `ngOnDestroy`), matching every `addEventListener`/`subscribe`/`setInterval` with a corresponding removal.
blocks.explanation: This is the standard framework-agnostic memory-leak triage process, and it's exactly why lifecycle cleanup hooks exist in every major frontend framework.

description: Senior/lead scenario: A bank-account object contains accountHolderName, mobileNumber, address, nominee and aadhaarNumber.
